title: Reading practice: The Lantern on Gull Rock and a Field-Trip Report
description: Eight reading items about a short story set in fog and an email report about a museum trip, practicing narrating, informing and explaining.

stimuli.title: The Lantern on Gull Rock
paragraphs: Ines had been on Gull Rock for only three days when the fog rolled in. Her uncle, the keeper of the small lighthouse, had gone to the mainland that morning to buy oil for the lamp. He had promised to be back before sunset. Now the sun was sinking, the fog was thickening, and his boat had not appeared.

At first, Ines tried to convince herself that nothing was wrong. She swept the stone steps, then she swept them again. Whenever the wind changed, she stopped and listened for the sound of an engine. Nothing came except the slow groan of the waves against the rocks.

Finally, she climbed the spiral stairs to the lamp room. The great lens was dark. Her uncle had shown her how to light it, but he had also warned her never to touch it alone. “It is not that the lamp is dangerous,” he had said. “It is that a keeper must be certain, because other people depend on the light.” Ines held the matches for a long moment. Her hands were not quite steady.

Out on the water, a low horn sounded, faint and uncertain. Somewhere a ship was searching for the channel, and the rocks around Gull Rock were famous for catching careless boats. Ines took a breath, remembered each step her uncle had taught her, and lit the lamp. A wide beam swept across the fog. Within an hour, a ship’s horn answered, and then another, and the sound grew steadily closer to the safe channel.

When her uncle finally climbed out of his small boat, soaked and out of breath, he looked up and saw the beam turning above him. He said nothing for a moment. Then he smiled. “I told you a keeper must be certain,” he said quietly. “Tonight, you were.”

stimuli.title: Email: What happened to Group 4 at the museum
paragraphs: Subject: What happened to Group 4 at the museum
You asked each group leader to send a short report about Thursday’s museum trip, so I am writing to explain what happened to my group.

We arrived at the front steps at 9:30, but our group’s tickets were with Ms. Lindgren, who had gone ahead with the other class. First, we waited near the fountain for about ten minutes. Then I checked the schedule and saw that she was supposed to meet us at the ticket desk, not on the steps. After I realized my mistake, we hurried inside. By the time we found her, the guided tour had already started, so we joined the group late.

I should have read the schedule carefully before we got off the bus. Next time, I will check the meeting point with my group before we leave. Although we missed the first five minutes of the tour, everyone in my group still finished the worksheet.

items.stem: What problem does Ines face at the beginning of the story?

options.text: She has lost the matches, and the lamp room is locked.
Her uncle has not come back, and the fog is getting thicker.
A ship has struck the rocks, and her uncle is on board.
Her uncle forbids her to light the lamp, and the lens is cracked.

distractors.a: The matches appear later, when Ines holds them in the lamp room, and she climbs to that room. The story never says she lost them or that the room is locked.
distractors.c: In the story a ship is only searching for the channel. The text never says that any ship hit the rocks, and her uncle is in a small boat.
distractors.d: He showed her how to light it. His warning was about touching the lens alone, and it is not the problem in paragraph 1. The lens is never cracked.

items.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the uncle promised to be back before sunset, but the sun was sinking, the fog was thickening, and his boat had not appeared.

support.clue: Reread paragraph 1. Look for what the uncle promised and for what is happening outside as the evening gets darker.
support.frame: At the beginning, Ines faces the problem that ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different story). “Kwame promised to meet his sister at four o’clock, but the bus stop was empty and it had started to rain.” The problem is a promise that is not kept while conditions get worse. Find the problem in your paragraph the same way.

misconceptions.d: confuses a later warning with the opening problem

facts: Heavy fog makes it hard to see, so ships can lose their way near rocks.

items.stem: Put these events from the story in the order they happen.

items.text: A low horn sounds from the water.
Ines’s uncle leaves for the mainland to buy lamp oil.
Her uncle climbs out of his small boat and sees the beam.
Ines sweeps the stone steps two times.
Ines climbs the spiral stairs to the lamp room.

items.explanation: The uncle leaves in the morning, Ines sweeps the steps while she waits, she climbs to the lamp room, a horn sounds on the water, she lights the lamp, and her uncle returns last.

support.clue: Look for time words and actions at the start of the paragraphs: that morning, at first, finally, and when her uncle finally returned.
support.model: Mentor example (a different story). “At dawn, Rafi packed his bag. Next, he walked to the harbor. After the ferry arrived, he climbed aboard. Finally, he waved goodbye.” Order words show the order of events. Use the story’s order words to place your events.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the uncle says, “a keeper must be certain, because other people depend on the light.” What does this tell the reader about how he sees a keeper’s job?

options.text: A keeper should avoid using the lamp whenever he or she feels nervous.
A keeper must be certain that the ships will find the harbor on their own.
Other people rely on a keeper, so he must be prepared and dependable.
A keeper must be certain that the weather will stay clear for the ships.

distractors.a: Ines is nervous but still lights the lamp, and her uncle praises her. Being certain means being prepared, not feeling calm.
distractors.b: The uncle says people depend on the light, which means ships need the keeper. They cannot find the harbor on their own.
distractors.d: Here “certain” means sure of one’s own actions. The lamp is needed because the weather is bad.

items.explanation: The uncle gives the reason after “because”: other people depend on the light, so a keeper has to be prepared and reliable.

support.clue: Read the sentence again, especially the words after “because.” Ask who else is affected by the keeper’s work.
support.frame: The uncle thinks a keeper must be ______ because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different job). “A pilot must check every instrument, because passengers depend on a safe flight.” The word “because” points to the reason a job needs great care. Look at what follows “because” in the uncle’s sentence.

items.stem: Choose the words that best complete the summary of causes and effects.

dropdown.template: The thick fog made it hard for ships to {1}. Ines lit the lamp even though she was {2}. As a result, the ships {3}.

options: turned back toward the open sea
moved closer to the safe channel
3.answer: moved closer to the safe channel

items.explanation: The fog hid the channel, Ines’s hands were not steady but she lit the lamp, and the sound of the horns grew closer to the safe channel.

support.clue: Reread paragraphs 3 and 4. Notice what the ship was searching for, how Ines’s hands felt, and what the sound of the horns did after the beam appeared.
support.model: Mentor example (a different situation). “Heavy snow covered the road signs, so the driver could not find the turn. The driver felt anxious but kept going slowly. As a result, the car reached the village safely.” Each blank asks for a cause, a feeling, or a result. Fill the blanks about the lighthouse the same way.

facts: Heavy fog makes it hard to see, so ships can lose their way near rocks.

items.stem: Which TWO sentences from the story give information about the weather and the sea near Gull Rock?

options.text: Her hands were not quite steady.
Now the sun was sinking, the fog was thickening, and his boat had not appeared.
Her uncle had shown her how to light it, but he had also warned her never to touch it alone.
Nothing came except the slow groan of the waves against the rocks.

distractors.a: This tells how Ines feels. It gives no information about the weather or the sea.
distractors.c: This gives information about the uncle’s instructions, not about the weather or the sea.

items.explanation: The sinking sun and thickening fog describe the weather, and the groaning waves describe the sea.

support.clue: Look for details about what you could see and hear outside: the sky, the air, and the water. Ignore details about what people feel or say.
support.frame: One detail about the weather is ______. One detail about the sea is ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different place). “The sky turned gray and a cold wind began to blow. Below the cliff, the waves crashed loudly on the sand.” The first sentence gives weather information, and the second gives sea information. Find two details of the same kinds in the story.

misconceptions.a: confuses a feeling with the setting

items.stem: Why does Daniela write this email to Mr. Okafor?

options.text: She wants to ask for tickets to another museum trip.
She wants to complain that the museum tour was too long.
She wants to invite him to join her group at the museum.
She wants to tell him what happened to her group on the trip.

distractors.a: Tickets are mentioned only as part of what went wrong. She does not ask for more.
distractors.b: She does not complain about the tour. She says her group missed its beginning.
distractors.c: She writes after the trip is over, so she cannot be inviting him to join it.

items.explanation: The first sentence of the message says Mr. Okafor asked each group leader for a report, so Daniela is writing to explain what happened to her group.

support.clue: Read the sentence that begins “You asked ...”. It tells what the teacher requested and why she is writing.
support.frame: Daniela is writing because Mr. Okafor asked her to ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different message). “Dear Coach, you asked each captain to send a list of players who can travel, so I am writing to share my team’s list.” The writer states the purpose right after the word “so.” Find the purpose sentence in the email.

misconceptions.c: misreads the time of the trip

items.stem: Match each time phrase from the email to the event it introduces.

left.text: By the time we found her

right.text: the guided tour had already started
the group waited near the fountain

items.explanation: Each time phrase introduces the event that follows it in the paragraph that begins “We arrived at the front steps.” Finishing the worksheet comes later, after “Although.”

support.clue: Find the paragraph that begins “We arrived at the front steps.” Each time phrase is followed by a comma and a clause that names the event.
support.model: Mentor example (a different story). “First, Aroha set the table. Then she lit the candles. By the time the guests arrived, the room was ready.” Here First goes with setting the table and Then goes with lighting the candles. Do the same with the email’s time phrases.

items.stem: Sort each statement from the email: is it part of the mix-up that happened first, or something that happened after the mix-up?

tokens.text: Daniela did not read the schedule carefully before getting off the bus.
The group hurried inside to look for Ms. Lindgren.
Ms. Lindgren was supposed to meet the group at the ticket desk, not on the steps.
The group missed the first five minutes of the tour.

items.explanation: Daniela’s mistake about the schedule and the real meeting place are the mix-up that happened first. Hurrying inside and missing five minutes of the tour happened after it.

support.clue: For each statement, ask: did it help cause the mix-up, or did it follow from it? Look at the paragraph that begins “We arrived at the front steps” and at the paragraph that begins “I should have read.”
support.frame: This is part of the mix-up because ______. This happened after because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different story). “The bike had a flat tire (why), so Ayo walked to school and arrived late (result).” A reason comes first and explains the result that follows. Sort the email’s statements the same way.
